searchDocs.title: What is new​
searchDocs.content: There is more here than a version bump, so let me go through it in the order I think you will actually notice it:  Modern modules. Built on the current d3 modules, shipped as ES modules, CommonJS, UMD and CDN builds, with an exports map and TypeScript typings for every chart. Vite, Rollup, esbuild and webpack all work out of the box, which was not true of v2 — every bundler had its own workaround, and I was tired of maintaining them.Smaller bundles. The build now targets ES2020, and Babel is gone entirely from @britecharts/core and @britecharts/wrappers — the core UMD bundle drops 12.7% (151,923 → 132,626 bytes) and the React bundle 14% (368 → 315 KB). You do not need to do anything for this one; a browser below the new target already needs a bundler or its own polyfills to run modern syntax at all, so nothing that worked before stops working now.One tooltip. tooltip and miniTooltip used to be two components with two sets of bugs. They are one now, and it never gets cut off at the chart's edges, follows the pointer smoothly, and behaves the same way whichever chart it is attached to.Negative values on the bar, stacked bar, grouped bar and brush charts, stacking down from zero. This has been the second-most-requested thing since 2019, and the reason it took this long is that I kept underestimating how much of the domain math assumed zero was the floor.Loading states for every chart, colorMap to name the colour of each category, animationDuration on every animated chart, and charts that are responsive by default.React 19 is tested end to end, not just claimed: the unit suite itself now runs on React 19, and the React package is also installed into a real React 19 project under StrictMode on every change. If you have been holding off upgrading because you weren't sure the wrappers would survive StrictMode's double-invoked effects, that is exactly what this checks.

searchDocs.title: Moving from version 2​
searchDocs.content: Most of the work is renaming, and I tried to keep it that way on purpose — a rewrite nobody can follow is worse than a major version nobody wants to install. The migration guide walks through every breaking change with a before and after for each. The ones you will hit first:  Imports. The charts are named exports of @britecharts/core (import { bar } from '@britecharts/core') instead of files under britecharts/dist/umd. The CommonJS, UMD and CDN paths are in the guide too.Loading states. loadingState() is gone; render the chart with isLoading(true) and a dataset, empty or not.Renamed accessors. locale is valueLocale on the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot; the value formatters of the grouped and stacked bar are numberFormat; the line and stacked area swap xAxisFormat and xAxisCustomFormat back to what their names say; aspectRatio is removed.Tooltips. The line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts now dispatch customMouseMove the same way every other chart does, as (dataPoint, [x, y], [width, height], colorMap). If you drive tooltip.update yourself, it still accepts the old argument order and warns once.exportChart returns a promise.  Version 2 ends at 2.18.2. I am not going to pretend I will keep patching it once 3.0 ships, so if you are on v2 and this list looks manageable, better to do it now than after a security report forces the question.

searchDocs.title: Where to start​
searchDocs.content: The installation and getting started tutorials build a first chart from scratch, and styling charts covers themes and CSS.The API reference has a page per chart and one for the tooltip.The Storybook shows every chart, in core and in React, with its options live — that is usually faster than reading accessor names off a page.

searchDocs.title: Tell us what breaks​
searchDocs.content: A beta is only useful if people actually try to break it, so please do. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected instead — the more specific, the faster I can act on it.  I will also say plainly what the contributing guide says: Britecharts needs maintainers. I have carried this release mostly on my own, and a 3.7k-star library with one person behind it is not a sustainable place to leave it. If any part of this codebase is something you would enjoy owning, that guide is where to start the conversation.

searchDocs.title: labelChart​
searchDocs.content: Gives a chart's svg the role, aria-label and <desc> that screen readers announce. The name is an attribute, not a <title>: browsers show an svg's<title> as a tooltip when the pointer rests on the chart. Run on every render: it reuses the <desc> it made the first time and only updates its text, so its id, and the attribute that points at it, stay stable.  Kind: global constant

searchDocs.title: prefersReducedMotion​
searchDocs.content: Whether the reader's system asks for reduced motion. Charts check it on every render, so isAnimated gives way to it, and a change to the setting applies from the next render. False where there is no matchMedia, as on a server or in jsdom.  Kind: global constant

searchDocs.title: What changed since the first beta​
searchDocs.content: When I announced the beta in September, I said it held more than a version bump. The betas since then have made the packages behave the way modern tooling expects. They also fixed the places where the charts said one thing and did another. Here is what you will notice:  One bundle per package, built with Vite. Version 2 published a file for every chart. Version 3 now publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle per package, plus ES modules for bundlers. Bundlers already drop the charts you do not import, so a file per chart saved nothing there. On a page with a script tag, one request is better than five.Real ES module packages. The three packages declare "type": "module", so import works in Node as well as in bundlers, with matching types for each way of loading. require still works and loads the CommonJS bundle, which now ends in .cjs.Charts that screen readers can name. Every chart gives its svg a role and an accessible name, "Bar chart" by default. Set a11yTitle to name it after what it shows. Set a11yDescription to add a sentence about what it means.Negative values in the scatter plot. Its value axis now runs below zero when the data does, and each circle's size shows the size of its value. That completes the negative values work: the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts all draw them.Typings that match the charts. I compared every chart's published types with what it does at run time, and fixed more than a hundred mismatches. Getters were declared as setters, callbacks had the wrong return type, and accessors were declared but never existed. If TypeScript accepts a call now, the chart does what the call says.Smaller fixes you may have hit. The brush honours locale and the stacked area honours numberFormat, which both used to do nothing. The scatter plot's zoom works again. The grouped and stacked bar tooltips no longer flicker when you move across the bars. Resting the pointer on a chart no longer pops up the browser's own tooltip. A chart's valueLocale no longer changes the numbers of every other chart on the page. A colorMap that names only some categories colours the rest from the palette.Tooltips that say what each chart needs. The charts name the fields of the data they send the tooltip differently. Some of them need the tooltip told where to look: topicLabel('values') for the stacked area, nameLabel('stack') or nameLabel('group') for the stacked and grouped bars, valueLabel('y') for the scatter plot. The tooltip reference and a new how-to list them per chart. Every story shows them in use.Leaner API pages and more recipes. Each accessor's heading starts with its name instead of exports., in the pages and in their tables of contents. The how-to guides gain recipes for per-category colours, number and date formats, loading states, animation, negative values and accessibility.In React, Tooltip infers its data type from its data prop, so its render callback type-checks without a cast. Seven settings the charts always had are now props, and prop-types is no longer a peer dependency.

searchDocs.title: What to check before you upgrade​
searchDocs.content: If you tried an earlier beta, five changes in this stretch can break your code. The migration guide covers each of them with a before and after:  Per-chart files are gone. Import the charts from the package, or load dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js and use the core global.CommonJS bundles end in .cjs. This matters only if you required a bundle by its path.The bullet chart and the sparkline no longer draw titles. Text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores your page's typography, so put the label in your own markup and pass the same text to a11yTitle.An accessor you have not set reads null, on every chart. Before, some charts returned undefined. A truthiness check works as before.The data-key accessors are gone. nameLabel, valueLabel, dateLabel and the rest no longer let a chart read your data under other keys. They had warned since version 2 that they would go. Rename the keys in your data to the ones the chart's data shape names, such as name and value. The tooltip keeps its own four.  If you are coming from version 2, the guide has the full list. Version 2 ends at 2.18.2.

searchDocs.title: What happens next​
searchDocs.content: Between now and 3.0.0, I only plan to fix bugs. The API is settled, so if something in it is wrong, now is the last cheap moment to say so. After 3.0.0 ships, changing it means another major version.  So please try this beta in a real project. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected. The Storybook shows every chart and its options, in core and in React. It is the fastest way to check whether something is a bug or a setting.  Britecharts still needs maintainers. If you would like to own part of it, the contributing guide is where to start.

searchDocs.title: getValueDomain ⇒ Array.<number>​
searchDocs.content: Builds the domain for a value axis so that it always contains zero.  Charts whose marks grow from a baseline need that baseline inside the domain, otherwise a negative value scales to a coordinate outside the range and the mark is drawn with a negative width or height, which SVG rejects.  For data that is entirely non-negative this returns [0, max].  Kind: global constant Returns: Array.<number> - [lower, upper], always spanning zero  Param	Type	Descriptionvalues	Iterable.<number>	Values the axis has to cover ratio	number	Headroom multiplier applied to the extent emptyDomainMax	number	Upper bound to use when every value is 0

searchDocs.title: getBaselineExtent ⇒ Object​
searchDocs.content: Where a mark that grows from the zero baseline starts, and how long it is.  Works for either axis: with a vertical scale start is a y and size a height, with a horizontal one they are an x and a width. Negative values come back on the other side of the baseline with a positive size, which is what SVG needs.  scale is typed structurally, as the number-to-number function this actually calls it as, rather than as a d3 ScaleLinear. That is both narrower about what is required and wider about what satisfies it: any of d3's continuous scales fits, and the helper never touches the rest of a scale's surface.  Kind: global constant Returns: Object - Where the mark starts and how long it is  Param	Type	Descriptionscale	function	Linear scale for the value axis value	number	Value to place

searchDocs.title: Scale~AxisScale : function​
searchDocs.content: What a chart calls on an axis scale, typed structurally rather than as a d3 scale class.  Several charts hold two different kinds of scale in one variable: xScale is a scaleLinear when the chart is horizontal and a scaleBand when it is vertical, and yScale is the mirror image. No single d3 class describes either, and the isHorizontal flag cannot narrow a module-level let.GridScale in grid.ts and getBaselineExtent's scale parameter in domain.ts already type scales this way, for the same reason -- narrower about what is required, wider about what satisfies it.  The call signature returns number | undefined because a band scale's does: it maps a category name and has nothing to return for a name outside its domain. bandwidth and ticks are optional because only one kind of scale has each.  Kind: inner typedef of Scale

searchDocs.title: Reading each chart's data point​
searchDocs.content: The charts do not all name the fields of the data point they dispatch the same way, so the tooltip has to be told where to look for some of them. Without these settings, a tooltip on these charts shows no rows, rows without their colours, or no value:  Chart	Configure the tooltip with	Whyline	nothing	its data point carries date and topics, the defaults stacked area	topicLabel('values')	its rows are under values stacked bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('stack')	its rows are under values, named by stack grouped bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('group')	its rows are under values, named by group scatter plot	valueLabel('y')	a point's value is its y (add nameLabel('x') to show x instead of its name) bar, donut, heatmap	nothing	their data points carry name and value  In React, Tooltip starts from topicLabel('values'), so the line chart is the one that needs a setting there: topicLabel="topics".

searchDocs.title: Key Features​
searchDocs.content: 🛠 Reusable - Configure your charts to create different looks and behaviors.🏗 Composable - Mix and match components to create insightful experiences.🌈 Great design - Clean and vivid looks to amaze your users.⚙️ Simple - The codebase is a regular D3.js code you can fork and modify.  Britecharts components have been written in ES2016 with a Test Driven methodology, so they are fully tested, and we are committed to keeping them that way.

searchDocs.title: Usage​
searchDocs.content: The typical use of Britecharts involves creating a chart using its simple API, then rendering it on a container that has previously had data applied to it. The code will look like this:   import { select } from 'd3-selection'; import { bar } from '@britecharts/core'; const barChart = bar(); const barContainer = select('.bar-chart-container'); const dataset = [...]; barChart .width(500) .height(300); barContainer.datum(dataset).call(barChart);   To use Britecharts with React, you will need to use the @britecharts/react package. Also, if you use Angular, check out ngx-britecharts and their demos. We also include a set of wrappers in @britecharts/wrappers that you can use to employ Britecharts with other web frameworks.

searchDocs.title: API​
searchDocs.content: All the components expose common API methods like width, height, and margin. Additionally, each component exposes specific methods you can find in the documentation:  API, Demo Line ChartAPI, Demo Bar ChartAPI, Demo Donut ChartAPI, Demo Stacked Bar ChartAPI, Demo Grouped Bar ChartAPI, Demo Bullet ChartAPI, Demo Brush ChartAPI, Demo Scatter PlotAPI, Demo Sparkline ChartAPI, Demo Stacked Area ChartAPI, Demo Mini Tooltip (the tooltip's single-value preset)API, Demo TooltipAPI, Demo Legend

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts components are distributed in UMD modules and ES modules, each one exposing a D3.js component written with the Reusable API pattern. To use any of the Britecharts modules, you will need to require the chart in your JS file using CommonJS modules, ES modules, or adding a <script> tag with the src pointing to the file or CDN bundle. You would also need to load the d3-selection submodule to select the chart container.   npm install --save @britecharts/core d3-selection # or pnpm add @britecharts/core d3-selection   Alternatively, you can load Britecharts from our CDN as we do in this demo page or play around in our CodePen demo projects.  Then, in your JavaScript module file you can now import and use charts:  import { bar } from '@britecharts/core'; import { select } from 'd3-selection'; const barChart = bar(); const container = select('#container'); const barData = [ { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 }, { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 }, { name: 'Intense', value: 4 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 } ]; barChart .margin({ left: 100 }) .isHorizontal(true) .height(400) .width(600); container.datum(barData).call(barChart);   Britecharts comes with a basic set of CSS styles that you would load with a <link> tag in your page's <head>.  <link rel="stylesheet" href="./node_modules/britecharts/dist/css/britecharts.css" />*   You can customize CSS using new styles. Check our Styling Britecharts tutorial to get started.

searchDocs.title: How to Create a Pull Request​
searchDocs.content: When you have a branch that you want to contribute back to Britecharts, you need to create a Pull Request(PR) to propose the addition of the code. Follow these steps:  When you're finished coding, git checkout mainRun git pull upstream main (note that your local main should always reflect upstream main)Run git checkout <your branch>Execute git rebase main & reconcile all conflictsMake sure everything looks OK codewise by running pnpm run checkPush the branch to your fork with git push origin <your branch>Create a new PR, filling the PR template, and adding a link to the original issue filed (if you see "unable to merge", please pull from your upstream and rebase again)Be patient while you wait for the maintainers to check it :)  If you are new to Open Source, you can learn how to create Pull Requests here.

searchDocs.title: How to Modify a Chart in @britecharts/core​
searchDocs.content: This how-to guide helps you in modifying a chart. We assume you already created an issue and got the green light form the maintainers of the project (or maybe you are working your fork if you are not contributing back to Britecharts).  We have created our charts with a Test-First approach, and we encourage you to keep it the same. However, you can also write tests later too. For a TDD workflow, the process of modifying a component would look like this:  Create a new branch for your modificationOn a new terminal, run pnpm run demos in the root folder and navigate to the chart's demo in storybookFind the test of the chart you want to modify in /packages/core/src/charts/<chartName> with at .spec.js extensionWrite a failing test for the API accessor or the feature you want to addOn a new terminal, run pnpm run test from the root folderCheck that the test failsWrite the code that would make that test pass on the chart located in /packages/core/src/charts/<chartName>. Please follow our API Guidelines.Make the test pass by writing the less amount of codeRefactor until you get a nice and clean codeAdd/update the JSDoc comments so that the proper documentation gets generated when you run pnpm run docsCheck the storybook demo to see the code in action (you can also add a new demo there if necessary)Create a pull request and ask the maintainers to review itOnce you have their OK, they will merge your pull request

searchDocs.title: How to Create a New Chart in @britecharts/core​
searchDocs.content: Adding a new chart is a bunch of work, but we hope that using the current code and documentation helps you in the process. The steps are:  Create a new branch for your componentOn a new terminal, run pnpm run demos to see the storybook running.Given that your new chart is chart-name, create a folder within /packages/core/src/charts named chart-name and in the same folder a new test file chart-name.spec.js.Create a new data builder file. Name it something like chartNameChartDataBuilder.js.In the chart folder, create a new chart file called chart-name.js.Create a <chartName>.stories.js file to hold a new demo for the new chart. Re-run the demos script to get it showing in the storybook.Export the new chart from packages/core/src/index.ts, with a camel case name, so it ships in the bundles.Go to your test file /packages/core/src/charts/chart-name.spec.js and, taking another test as an example, copy over pieces until you have the first test case.Add one test and make it fail by calling pnpm run test or keep the tests running with pnpm run test:watch.Keep on coding according to our API GuidelinesOnce you think you are close to having something working, start adding JSDoc comments to your codeGenerate your docs with pnpm run docs and manually test the API definition in the docs site.Create a pull request with your branch and ping one of the core maintainers to get it reviewedOnce you have addressed all the comments and got the green light, the maintainers will merge the PR

searchDocs.title: How to Customize the Chart's Colors​
searchDocs.content: Follow these steps to customize Britecharts' charts to use different color schemas:  Find out if your chart supports the .colorSchema() configuration, if so, keep on readingCheck the Color Palettes demo page and find a palette you likeImport the colors helper at the top of your fileSet the color palette with .colorSchema(colors.colorSchemas.orange) or with any other color schemaDraw the chart  For readers with colour blindness, use colors.colorSchemas.okabeIto. Its eight colours, from Okabe and Ito's palette, stay distinct with the common kinds of colour blindness. Black comes last, so charts with up to seven categories never draw a series in black. Its yellow, orange and sky blue are light on a white background, so the palette suits filled marks such as bars and donut slices better than thin lines. Colour shouldn't be the only thing that tells series apart: a legend or labels help every reader.  Note that in some charts we can only configure a gradient. Use the colorGradients object instead of colorSchemas within the colors helper. You can explore other options in the source code of the colors file.

searchDocs.title: Give each category its own colour​
searchDocs.content: A palette assigns colours in order, so a category's colour changes when the data does. To pin one colour to each category, pass colorMap an object from category to colour:  barChart.colorMap({ Shiny: '#39c2c9', Blazing: '#fcc870', });   A category the map leaves out keeps its palette colour. Each chart matches the keys against one field of its data:  Chart	colorMap keys matchBar, donut, scatter plot, stacked area	name Line	name, the topic's identifier (not topicName) Stacked bar	stack Grouped bar	group  The legend takes colorMap too: pass it the same object so its entries match the chart. In React, colorMap is a prop with the same shape.

searchDocs.title: How to Add a Tooltip to a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Every chart dispatches the same three events, and the tooltip has a handler for each:  Create the tooltip: tooltip() for the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts, which list one row per topic, or miniTooltip() for the bar, donut, heatmap and scatter plot, which show one valueConnect the chart's customMouseOver, customMouseMove and customMouseOut events to the tooltip's show, update and hideTell the tooltip where the chart keeps its data, if the table below lists a setting for itDraw the chart, then call the tooltip on the chart's .metadata-group (for the line and stacked area, on .metadata-group .vertical-marker-container)  const stackedBarChart = stackedBar(); const chartTooltip = tooltip() .topicLabel('values') .nameLabel('stack'); stackedBarChart .on('customMouseOver', chartTooltip.show) .on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update) .on('customMouseOut', chartTooltip.hide); select('.js-chart').datum(data).call(stackedBarChart); select('.js-chart .metadata-group').datum([]).call(chartTooltip);   The charts do not all name the fields of the data point they send the tooltip the same way, so some need a setting. Without it, the tooltip shows no rows, rows without their colours, or no value:  Chart	Tooltip settings	React Tooltip propsLine	none	topicLabel="topics" Stacked area	topicLabel('values')	none Stacked bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('stack')	nameLabel="stack" Grouped bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('group')	nameLabel="group" Scatter plot	valueLabel('y')	valueLabel="y" Bar, donut, heatmap	none	none  React's Tooltip starts from topicLabel('values'), which is why the line chart is the one that needs a prop there. The tooltip reference describes each setting, and the Storybook shows each chart with its tooltip configured.

searchDocs.title: How to Format Numbers and Dates for Your Language​
searchDocs.content: Three settings control how values read. They do different things, so check which one a chart has in its API reference:  numberFormat takes a d3-format specifier, such as ',.2f' for two decimals with a thousands separator, or '.0%' for a percentage. It formats the values on the chart's axes and labels; the tooltip has a numberFormat of its own.valueLocale takes a d3-format locale definition and sets the separators and currency those values use. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot charts have it. The definition needs at least decimal, thousands, grouping and currency, or the chart throws.locale takes a language tag such as 'fr-FR', and localizes the dates in the tooltip and the brush with Intl.DateTimeFormat.  barChart .numberFormat(',.2f') .valueLocale({ decimal: ',', thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ['', ' €'], }); // The axis reads 1.000,00 instead of 1,000.00   Negative numbers use the typographic minus sign (−), as d3-format does. To get the ASCII hyphen back, add minus: '-' to the locale definition.  Each chart keeps its valueLocale to itself, so two charts on a page can use different ones.

searchDocs.title: How to Show a Loading State​
searchDocs.content: Every data chart can draw a skeleton in its own shape while the data loads:  Set isLoading(true) and draw the chart with whatever data you have, even an empty arrayWhen the data arrives, set isLoading(false) and draw the chart again with it  barChart.isLoading(true); container.datum([]).call(barChart); fetchData().then((data) => { barChart.isLoading(false); container.datum(data).call(barChart); });   In React, pass isLoading together with the data you have, an empty array included, and set it to false when the data arrives. With data={null}, the component draws nothing at all, skeleton included.

searchDocs.title: How to Animate a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Charts draw without animation by default. Set isAnimated(true) to animate them as they draw, and animationDuration to set how long that takes, in milliseconds (1200 by default):  lineChart.isAnimated(true).animationDuration(600);   animationDuration does nothing while isAnimated is false. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area, donut, heatmap, scatter plot, sparkline and brush charts animate. React components take both as props.  A reader whose system asks for reduced motion (the prefers-reduced-motion setting) sees every chart drawn without animation, whatever isAnimated is set to. Charts check it each time they draw, so changing the setting applies from the next render. isAnimated() still reads back the value you set.

searchDocs.title: How to Export a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Call exportChart with a filename to download the chart as it is drawn. The filename picks the format: one ending in .svg downloads an svg file, and any other a png. An optional second argument adds a title at the top:  barChart.exportChart('visits.svg', 'Visits by month'); barChart.exportChart('visits.png');   The svg keeps the chart's styles inlined, so it looks the same in a design tool or a document, and it stays sharp at any size. exportChart returns a promise that resolves once the download starts. In React, the grouped bar, heatmap, line, sparkline, stacked area and stacked bar components take the filename as their exportChart prop.

searchDocs.title: How to Chart Negative Values​
searchDocs.content: The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts draw negative values with no setting to turn on:  The bar charts draw bars below, or to the left of, a zero baseline, and a stacked bar stacks its negative parts down from zero.The scatter plot's value axis runs below zero when the data does, and a circle's size shows the size of its value, so -50 draws as large as 50.  The line and stacked area charts plot negative values as they are. Axis labels for negative numbers use the typographic minus sign: see how to format numbers to change it.

searchDocs.title: How to Make a Chart Accessible​
searchDocs.content: Every chart gives its svg a role and a name that screen readers announce: "Bar chart" by default. Name it after what it shows, and add a sentence about what it means:  barChart .a11yTitle('Monthly visits') .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');   The name goes in an aria-label, so browsers do not show it as a tooltip on hover. React components take a11yTitle and a11yDescription as props.

searchDocs.title: Label a bullet chart or a sparkline​
searchDocs.content: The bullet chart and the sparkline draw only their data, with no title: text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores the page's typography. Put the label in your own markup, next to the chart, and give screen readers the same words:  <h3>CPU load <small>GHz</small></h3> <div class="js-bullet-chart"></div>   bulletChart.a11yTitle('CPU load, GHz'); select('.js-bullet-chart').datum(data).call(bulletChart);

searchDocs.title: How to Configure Time Scales​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts has some logic to try guessing the best date format on time series charts from the time period of the dataset. As we haven't bulletproofed this algorithm, and sometimes users want specific formats, we also expose configuration options to set custom formats.  The next steps apply to time series charts like the line chart, stacked area chart and brush chart:  Render the chart using the default settings, see if the x-axis format is satisfactory. If not, keep on reading.Check the chart's reference to find out the configuration options, for example, the line chart referenceCheck the options within the axisTimeCombinations object of the chart instance:  console.log('combinations', line.axisTimeCombinations); // Returns { MINUTE_HOUR: 'minute-hour', HOUR_DAY: 'hour-daymonth', DAY_MONTH: 'day-month', MONTH_YEAR: 'month-year', CUSTOM: 'custom' }   Set the xAxisFormat parameter to a value from the ones below (except 'custom')Draw the chart and see if it meets your criteria. If not, try with other time combination. If still doesn't feel right, see next step.Set the xAxisFormat parameter to the value 'custom'Set the xAxisCustomFormat parameter to a valid D3.js time format specifier string. For example: line.xAxisCustomFormat('%H')Play around with different specifiers until finding something that works. You can experiment in this block example.  Remember that for increased accuracy, all date formats in Britecharts should be provided in ISO 8601 Extended Format.

searchDocs.title: General Considerations​
searchDocs.content: Variable and accessor names should be camel cased (eg. "shouldBeCamelCase"), and we try to use only one word that is the same as the internal variable we are using. Variables are nouns, while commands are verbs.  For example: height, width, margin, title.

searchDocs.title: Variable and function names length​
searchDocs.content: We will follow the 'Scope Rule':  Variable names: short in small scopes (d)long in large scopes (percentageLabelMargin) Functions names: short in large scopes like public commands (hide, width)long in small scopes (drawVerticalExtendedLine)

searchDocs.title: Event dispatchers​
searchDocs.content: The custom events that are attached to the charts always are prefixed with ‘on’.  As in: .on('customHover')

searchDocs.title: Booleans​
searchDocs.content: We want them to be predicates. They are prefixed with one of the following:  shouldhasis  As in: isAnimated, hasFixedHighlightedSlice.

searchDocs.title: Commands​
searchDocs.content: Commands must be verbs and be constructed into a single word if possible  As in: hide, show, exportChart

searchDocs.title: Data labels​
searchDocs.content: For API entries that configure the keys of the input data, we use the property name and the suffix ‘label’.  As in: dateLabel, valueLabel

searchDocs.title: Formats​
searchDocs.content: A simple name with the property name and ‘format’ suffix.  As in: numberFormat, xLabelFormat

searchDocs.title: Ticks and Axis​
searchDocs.content: We use the axis name followed by the 'axis' and ‘ticks’ suffix:  As in: xTicks, yTicks

searchDocs.title: Usage​
searchDocs.content: Every chart in @britecharts/react is a function component: you pass in some props, and it renders a chart.  import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react'; const data = [ { name: 'Vibrant', value: 2, }, { name: 'Opalescent', value: 4, }, { name: 'Shining', value: 3, }, ]; <Bar data={data} width={400} isHorizontal />   Check our Storybook for more examples and check the source to copy/paste code.

searchDocs.title: Loading data​
searchDocs.content: data is required. Pass null while it loads: nothing is drawn until it arrives, and the chart is drawn as soon as it does. Leaving data out, or passing undefined, is an error (and a type error, too).  <Bar data={isLoading ? null : data} />

searchDocs.title: Updating a chart​
searchDocs.content: A chart is redrawn when its props change, and only then. On every render the data and each configuration value are compared with what was last drawn, so a re-render with the same props costs nothing. The consequence is that the data has to be a new array or object to be redrawn: mutating it in place and re-rendering with the same reference does nothing.  setData([...data, newPoint]); // redraws data.push(newPoint); setData(data); // does not: same array, nothing changed

searchDocs.title: No instance, no ref​
searchDocs.content: Function components have no instance to point a ref at, so a ref on a chart is not accepted (the typings say so). A chart is drawn into a <div> the component owns, and removes what it drew when it unmounts.

searchDocs.title: Tooltips​
searchDocs.content: A Tooltip wraps the chart it decorates: give it a render prop that returns the chart, and pass on the props it hands you, which are what connect the two.  The charts name the fields of their data points differently, so some of them need the tooltip told where to look:  Chart	Tooltip propsLine	topicLabel="topics" StackedArea	none StackedBar	nameLabel="stack" GroupedBar	nameLabel="group" ScatterPlot	valueLabel="y" Bar, Donut	none  Without them, the tooltip shows no rows (line), rows without their colours (stacked and grouped bar) or no value (scatter plot).  import { Line, Tooltip } from '@britecharts/react'; <Tooltip data={data} render={(props) => <Line {...props} />} topicLabel="topics" title="A title" />

searchDocs.title: Responsive charts​
searchDocs.content: ResponsiveContainer hands its render prop the width it has measured, and measures again when the window is resized. withResponsiveness does the same for a component you wrap, as its width prop (a width you pass yourself wins).  import { Line, ResponsiveContainer, withResponsiveness } from '@britecharts/react'; <ResponsiveContainer render={({ width }) => <Line data={data} width={width} />} /> const ResponsiveLine = withResponsiveness(Line); <ResponsiveLine data={data} />

searchDocs.title: API​
searchDocs.content: Each component's API is a reflection of Britecharts charts and their APIs. They also have a bunch of React specific props, and there are some changes due to the declarative way of building with React.  For example, if we need to check the options of a bar chart, you will first check the bar chart's API in the main project API reference page.  Every Britecharts chart has a component:  Bar charts (API)Brush charts (API)Bullet charts (API)Grouped Bar charts (API)Donut charts (API)Heatmaps (API)Line charts (API)Scatter Plots (API)Sparkline charts (API)Stacked Area charts (API)Stacked Bar charts (API)Tooltips (API), wrapping the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts with a list of values, and the bar, scatter plot and heatmap charts with a single value (the mini tooltip)Legends (API)The ResponsiveContainer component and the withResponsiveness function, described above  These components were previously hosted in the britecharts-react repository, but became a package with Britecharts V3.

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: To install run:  pnpm add @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers @britecharts/react   Or, with npm:  npm i --save @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers @britecharts/react   Britecharts-React is available as an NPM module or through CDN links (in different formats or a bundle).  Import the components from the package: bundlers get ES modules, and require('@britecharts/react') gets the UMD bundle. The React consumer in the integration package shows every way of loading it, and is what CI runs.

searchDocs.title: Supported React versions​
searchDocs.content: peerDependencies requires react and react-dom >=16.8: the components use hooks, which arrived in that release. What is actually verified on every commit:  React 19, by the unit tests, which now run on React Testing Library, and in a real browser: CI packs the package the way a release does, installs it into a React 19 project, and loads it in production and in a development build under StrictMode, which runs every effect's setup, cleanup and setup again.  React 17 and 18 are expected to work and are not exercised. If you hit a version-specific problem on an older React, please open an issue.

searchDocs.title: Acknowledgments​
searchDocs.content: For this project, we have followed the approach called ‘Mapping Lifecycle methods’ based on Nicholas Hery's article: a chart's create, update and destroy are called from the component's mount, update and unmount, which one internal hook now does for every chart. We want to recognize all the contributors in the parent project Britecharts.

searchDocs.content: Documentation HomepageContributing GuideCode of Conduct

searchDocs.title: Contribute​
searchDocs.content: When Britecharts adds a chart, check out our how-to guide for creating new charts to bring it to React. Check also the contributing guide if you want to help.  Note that the aim of this project is to allow the usage of Britecharts within your React applications. For that, we are ‘wrapping’ Britecharts with @britecharts/wrappers. This means that any new features need to first be implemented on Britecharts. Only then you could update the props and logic that passes in the configuration.

searchDocs.title: TypeScript​
searchDocs.content: The package is written in TypeScript, and its type declarations are generated from the components at build time. Each component's props type is exported from the package root (BarChartProps, LineProps and so on), and CI compiles a TypeScript project against the packed package.

searchDocs.title: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
Migration Steps​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Most of the migration tasks involve changing accessor names, but there are also changes in how we load the modules. Follow these steps to get your application updated in no time:

searchDocs.title: Breaking changes​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Update the way you load the charts  We moved Britecharts internally from the outdated AMD modules into ES Modules, which changed how you will import the components. See below some examples:  // Version 2 // For ES modules import bar from 'britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min'; // For AMD and CommonJS modules const LineChart = require('britecharts/umd/line.min'); // Version 3 // As ES modules import { bar } from '@britecharts/core'; // As CommonJS modules const { bar } = require('@britecharts/core');   The stylesheets move too. britecharts/dist/css/britecharts.min.css is now @britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css, and each chart's own stylesheet is under @britecharts/core/dist/styles/charts/.  You can also check more ways of loading (CommonJS, UMD and CDN) in the vanilla consumer of our integration tests, which CI runs against every change  Change how you show loading states  Search for any use of the 'loadingState' accessor for getting the loading state, and render the chart with 'isLoading' as true and a valid dataset (it can be empty).  // Version 2 barContainer.html(barChart.loadingState()) // Version 3 barChart .width(containerWidth) .height(300) .isAnimated(true) .isLoading(true); barContainer.datum(dataset).call(barChart);   Use 'valueLocale' to format values  You must use the 'valueLocale' accessor to set the locale object (see the d3-format docs) of the component´s rendered values (axes ticks, numerical values, etc.).  Before, this used to be ´locale´ in the bar, grouped bar, scatted bar, and scatter plot.  // Version 2 barChart .locale({ thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ["$", ""], decimal: "." }) //...other configurations // Version 3 barChart .valueLocale({ thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ["$", ""], decimal: "." }) //...other configurations   In contrast, for time series charts (lineChart, stackedAreaChart), we use 'locale' to pass the language tag for the tooltip to localize the date. It uses Intl.DateTimeFormat, for compatibility and support.  Swap the use 'xAxisCustomFormat' and 'xAxisFormat' on brush charts  Whenever you were using 'xAxisCustomFormat' in a brush chart, now you should use 'xAxisFormat', and viceversa.  // Version 2 brush .xAxisCustomFormat('custom') .xAxisFormat('%A'); // Version 3 brush .xAxisCustomFormat('%A') .xAxisFormat('custom');   This made this configuration consistent with the line and stacked area charts.  Use 'numberFormat' in bar charts  Search for uses of 'valueLabelFormat' and change them to 'numberFormat':  // Version 2 groupedBarChart .valueLabelFormat(',s') // other configurations // Version 3 groupedBarChart .numberFormat(',s') // other configurations   The 'numberFormat' configuration is available for the bar, bullet, donut, grouped bar, stacked-bar, legend, line, mini-tooltip, and tooltip components.  Stop using 'aspectRatio' to set charts' dimensions  We eliminated the 'aspectRatio' accessor from our charts. Instead, use the 'width' and 'height' attributes to set a explicit size and leave the chart to respond to container width changes.  // Version 2 lineChart .width(100) .aspectRatio('0.5'); // Version 3 lineChart .width(100) .height(50)   Expect the typographic minus sign in negative axis labels  Britecharts v3 runs on the current d3 modules, and d3-format changed its default minus sign from the ASCII hyphen (-, U+002D) to the typographic minus (−, U+2212). Negative values on axes and in tooltips now render with the latter.  Nothing to change unless you assert on that text — snapshot tests and string comparisons against axis labels will need updating. If you would rather keep the ASCII hyphen, set it through a value locale on the charts that have one (the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot). The definition needs decimal, thousands, grouping and currency as well:  barChart.valueLocale({ decimal: '.', thousands: ',', grouping: [3], currency: ['$', ''], minus: '-', });   Use the d3 v7 modules alongside Britecharts  Britecharts v3 runs on the d3 v7 generation of the d3-* modules. They are dependencies of @britecharts/core, so installing it from npm installs them, and the ES module and dist/umd builds load them from there rather than bundling them. If your own code uses d3 together with Britecharts, upgrade it to v7 at the same time. The CDN builds under dist/cdn bundle their own copy of d3 and need nothing else on the page.  The two d3 modules Britecharts used that are now deprecated upstream, d3-collection and d3-voronoi, have been replaced internally by d3-array and d3-delaunay. They are no longer dependencies.  Replace the 'dataByTopic' line chart data shape  The line chart no longer accepts the dataByTopic array it required up to 2.10.1. It has taken a flat data array since then, and that is now the only shape it accepts. Passing dataByTopic throws.  // Version 2 lineChart.datum({ dataByTopic: [ { topicName: 'San Francisco', topic: 123, dates: [ { date: '2017-01-16T16:00:00-08:00', value: 1 }, { date: '2017-01-17T16:00:00-08:00', value: 2 } ] } ] }); // Version 3 lineChart.datum({ data: [ { topicName: 'San Francisco', name: 123, date: '2017-01-16T16:00:00-08:00', value: 1 }, { topicName: 'San Francisco', name: 123, date: '2017-01-17T16:00:00-08:00', value: 2 } ] });   One entry per point instead of points nested under each topic, and the topic identifier moves from topic to name. Britecharts groups the data internally, so nothing else about how you configure the chart changes.  If you have data in the old shape, this converts it:  const toFlatData = ({ dataByTopic }) => dataByTopic.flatMap((topic) => topic.dates.map(({ date, value }) => ({ topicName: topic.topicName, name: topic.topic, date, value, })) );   Update custom tooltip handlers on the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts  Every chart now dispatches customMouseMove with the same payload: the hovered data point, its anchor [x, y] in pixels relative to the chart's drawing area, the chart's [width, height], and, from these four charts, the map of topic names to colours. Before, they dispatched (dataPoint, colorMap, x, y). If you wire the tooltip directly, nothing changes; a handler of your own that reads the arguments by position has to take the new order. tooltip.update still accepts the old order in 3.x and warns once.  // Version 2 lineChart.on('customMouseMove', function (dataPoint, colorMap, x, y) { chartTooltip.update(dataPoint, colorMap, x, y); trackHover(dataPoint, x); }); // Version 3 lineChart.on('customMouseMove', function (dataPoint, [x, y], size, colorMap) { chartTooltip.update(dataPoint, [x, y], size, colorMap); trackHover(dataPoint, x); }); // Either version lineChart.on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update);   With that, tooltip and miniTooltip are one component: tooltip shows a list or a single value by the shape of the data point (or as told by layout), and miniTooltip is tooltip().layout('single').title('').numberFormat('.2f'). The tooltip now keeps itself inside the chart, follows the pointer (the stacked and grouped bar charts show it over a bar only), and its tooltipOffset default is { x: 0, y: 0 } (it was { x: 0, y: -55 }, for a placement that no longer exists). xAxisValueType defaults to 'auto', which shows dates as dates, numbers as numbers and category names as they are; set 'date' or 'number' to force one, as before. In React, Tooltip's customMouseMove callback receives the new order, and Tooltip now wraps the bar, scatter plot and heatmap charts too.  Replace the Step chart  The Step chart is removed from every package: the step export of @britecharts/core, its StepWrapper and the React Step component, with their stylesheets and builds. A bar chart draws the same data.  Transpile for older browsers yourself  The builds now target ES2020 instead of ES5. Every current browser runs them as they are. If you support a browser older than that, transpile Britecharts in your own build, as you would any package that ships modern syntax.  Move from britecharts-react to @britecharts/react  The React components are published as @britecharts/react, and they work differently in a few ways you may rely on:  // Version 2 import { Bar } from 'britecharts-react'; // Version 3 import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react';   React 16.8 or later is required, since the components are now function components built on hooks. They have no instances any more, so a ref on a chart component is not accepted.A chart redraws only when its props change. If you update your data by mutating it in place, pass a new array or object instead.data is required. Pass null while it loads: the chart draws nothing until the data arrives.false, 0 and '' now reach the chart, so isLoading={false} ends a loading state. Leave a prop out, or pass undefined, to keep the chart's default.PropTypes are gone. Each component's props type is exported from the package root (BarChartProps, LineProps and so on) for TypeScript projects.StackedBar's nameLabelFormat prop is removed. No chart had that setting, so passing it threw.axisTimeCombinations is no longer a prop of Line, StackedArea or Tooltip. Import the axisTimeCombinations constant from the package and pass one of its values to xAxisFormat.  Label bullet charts and sparklines outside the chart  The bullet chart no longer draws a title and subtitle, and the sparkline no longer draws a title. Text drawn inside the svg cannot wrap, clips at the chart's edge and does not follow the page's typography, so these charts now draw only the data. The customTitle and customSubtitle accessors and the title and subtitle data fields of the bullet chart are removed, as are the sparkline's titleText and titleTextStyle. The React Bullet and Sparkline components drop the matching props.  Put the label in your own markup next to the chart, and give screen readers the chart's name with a11yTitle:  // Version 2 bulletChart.customTitle('CPU 1').customSubtitle('GHz'); sparklineChart.titleText('Signups'); // Version 3 // <h3>CPU 1 <small>GHz</small></h3> above the chart's container bulletChart.a11yTitle('CPU 1, GHz'); sparklineChart.a11yTitle('Signups');   The legend still draws its own labels.  Load one bundle instead of a file per chart  Version 2 published a UMD file for each chart, like britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min.js. Version 3 publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle with every chart, and ES modules for bundlers. Bundlers keep only the charts you import, so a per-chart file saves nothing there. On a page with a script tag, load the CDN bundle, which includes d3, and use the core global:  <!-- Version 2 --> <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min.js"></script> <script>const barChart = britecharts.bar();</script> <!-- Version 3 --> <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script> <script>const barChart = core.bar();</script>   The colors come with the bundle as core.colors. The per-chart stylesheets under dist/styles/charts/ are still published. @britecharts/wrappers and @britecharts/react also publish only their bundles: import the wrappers and components from the package, or use the wrappers and react globals.  The packages are ES modules ("type": "module"), so they load with import in Node as well as in bundlers. require still works and gets the CommonJS bundle, which is now a .cjs file. If you required a bundle by its path, update the extension: @britecharts/core/dist/umd/bundle/core.bundled.min.js is now core.bundled.min.cjs, and likewise for wrappers and react. The CDN bundle keeps its .js name.  Expect null from an accessor you have not set  An accessor that has not been set now reads null on every chart. Before, the same accessor read null on some charts and undefined on others: yAxisLabel on the grouped bar, stacked bar, scatter plot and stacked area, xAxisLabel on the scatter plot, numberFormat on the donut, line and stacked area, and locale on the line, stacked area and tooltip.  A truthiness check works as before. Update code that compares with === undefined, and TypeScript code that annotated the old type: the getters are typed T | null.  // Version 2 if (lineChart.numberFormat() === undefined) { /* ... */ } // Version 3 if (lineChart.numberFormat() === null) { /* ... */ }   Name your data's keys as the charts expect  The accessors that let a chart read its data under other keys are removed: nameLabel and valueLabel on the bar chart, groupLabel, nameLabel and valueLabel on the grouped bar, stackLabel, nameLabel and valueLabel on the stacked bar, dateLabel, topicLabel and valueLabel on the line chart, dateLabel, keyLabel and valueLabel on the stacked area, and dateLabel and valueLabel on the sparkline. They warned that they were deprecated since version 2. The React components drop the matching props.  If you used them, rename the keys in your data to the ones each chart's data shape names, such as name and value for the bar chart:  // Version 2 barChart.nameLabel('letter').valueLabel('frequency'); barContainer.datum([{ letter: 'A', frequency: 0.08 }]).call(barChart); // Version 3 const data = rows.map(({ letter, frequency }) => ({ name: letter, value: frequency })); barContainer.datum(data).call(barChart);   The tooltip keeps its dateLabel, nameLabel, topicLabel and valueLabel: it reads the data points of several charts, and they use different keys.

searchDocs.title: New features​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Start using TypeScript with Britecharts.  You can now use Britecharts in your TypeScript projects! The packages are written in TypeScript, and their type declarations are generated from that source, so they always match what the charts do. Import the types from the package root: each chart's data shape and module type from @britecharts/core, and each component's props from @britecharts/react.  Stop re-rendering charts when the viewport width changes.  In version 2 and our demos, we recommended listening to viewport width changes and re-render charts with the updated container width. This wasn't necessary, as SVGs provide a viewBox property that allows us to make our charts fully responsive out of the box. That's how Britecharts works starting version 3, so say bye-bye to those window 'resize' listeners!  Use 'colorMap' to select the colors you want for each data category.  One common request of our users was to specify the colors for each category on the different Britecharts components. Now you can! Use the "colorMap" property to specify a hash map between category names and HEX colors.  Specify the duration of animations with 'animationDuration'  Most Britecharts' components have animations that you can activate with the 'isAnimated' configuration. Since version 3, you can also set the duration of those animations in milliseconds with the 'animationDuration' accessor.  Rely on one tooltip for every chart  tooltip renders the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts' lists and the bar, scatter plot, heatmap and donut charts' single values; maxEntries caps the rows, layout forces a layout, xAxisValueType('category') shows a category key as it is. customClick on the stacked and grouped bar charts carries the clicked bar's own data as a third argument.  Chart negative values  The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and brush charts draw negative values, below or to the left of a zero baseline. They used to throw on a negative datum. The scatter plot's value axis now runs below zero when the data does, and each circle's size shows the magnitude of its value. Before, points with a negative value were not drawn.  Show a loading state on every chart  isLoading now covers every data chart, including the bullet, heatmap and scatter plot, each with a skeleton in its own shape.  Name your charts for screen readers  Every chart gives its svg a role and an accessible name, so a screen reader announces it as an image called, for example, "Bar chart". Set a11yTitle to name it after what it shows, and a11yDescription to add a sentence that screen readers read after the name. The React components take both as props.  barChart .a11yTitle('Monthly visits') .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');

searchDocs.title: Usage​
searchDocs.content: @britecharts/wrappers components expose a simple API to allow its use in frontend frameworks. This API contains three methods: create, update, and destroy.  To use them, you will pass a configuration object following the Britecharts core component API and a container:  import { BarWrapper } from '@britecharts/wrappers'; const container = document.querySelector('.container'); const data = [ { name: 'Vibrant', value: 2, }, { name: 'Opalescent', value: 4, }, { name: 'Shining', value: 3, }, ]; const configuration = { width: 400, margin: {left: 10}, }; const barInstance = BarWrapper.create(container, data, configuration); //... BarWrapper.update(container, newData, {}, barInstance);   The wrappers include a lightweight configuration and container validation.  A configuration value of undefined or null means "not set" and the chart keeps its own default. Any other value is applied, including the falsy ones: false, 0 and '' reach the chart, so a setting can be turned back off with { isLoading: false }.  In theory, you shouldn't be using this wrappers by themselves, but you might prefer this API (more OO-like) for your vanilla JavaScript projects.

searchDocs.title: API​
searchDocs.content: The API of the wrappers has only three methods: create, update and destroy. Note that each component wrapper's configuration options is a reflection of Britecharts charts' APIs.

searchDocs.title: Create​
searchDocs.content: Creates a new Britechart chart and returns its instance.  Signature:<Wrapper>.create(HTMLElement, <ChartDataShape>, <ConfigurationObject>) => BritechartChart  Example:  const barInstance = BarWrapper.create(container, data, configuration);

searchDocs.title: Update​
searchDocs.content: Updates a chart with new data or configuration.  Signature:<Wrapper>.update(HTMLElement, <ChartDataShape>, <ConfigurationObject>, BritechartChart) => BritechartChart  Example:  BarWrapper.update(container, newData, {}, barInstance);

searchDocs.title: Destroy​
searchDocs.content: Removes the chart's svg from the container, so the container can be used again (a create after a destroy draws exactly one chart). It only removes that svg: never the container itself, which a framework may own, nor anything else inside it.  Signature:<Wrapper>.destroy(HTMLElement) => void  Example:  BarWrapper.destroy(container);   TooltipWrapper.destroy has its own contract: it removes the tooltip from inside the element and never an svg, because a tooltip is created inside the chart it decorates and destroyed against the element around it.

searchDocs.title: Availability​
searchDocs.content: Every chart in @britecharts/core has a wrapper: BarWrapper, BrushWrapper, BulletWrapper, DonutWrapper, GroupedBarWrapper, HeatmapWrapper, LegendWrapper, LineWrapper, ScatterPlotWrapper, SparklineWrapper, StackedAreaWrapper and StackedBarWrapper, plus TooltipWrapper for the tooltip.

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: To install run:  pnpm add @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers   Or, with npm:  npm i --save @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers

searchDocs.title: Roadmap​
searchDocs.content: Our idea for the short term is to update this package to use TypeScript natively. Let us know if you want to help with it.

searchDocs.title: Building the packages​
searchDocs.content: Each published package is built from pnpm build in its folder, or all three at once with pnpm build:packages at the root. Babel writes the ES modules file by file and only strips the TypeScript types, and tsc writes the declarations. Core's UMD bundle, CDN bundle and stylesheets come from vite build with packages/core/vite.config.js, one run per mode. Wrappers' UMD and CommonJS bundles come from one vite build with packages/wrappers/vite.config.js. React's UMD bundle comes from vite build with packages/react/vite.config.js. The Storybooks run on Storybook 10's Vite builders, each with its own .storybook/vite.config.mjs. The output targets ES2020.  What comes out of packages/core/dist:  Path	Contentsumd/bundle/core.bundled.min.cjs	Every chart in one UMD bundle: the package's main, and what require loads. types-cjs/	The type declarations again, marked CommonJS, for the require condition. cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js	The same, built for a <script> tag, with d3 bundled in. styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css	Every stylesheet. styles/charts/common.min.css, styles/charts/<chart>.min.css	The shared styles, and one file per chart to use alongside them.  The wrappers package emits a UMD and a CommonJS bundle; the React package a UMD bundle. pnpm build at the root builds the three packages, this site and the Storybooks.

searchDocs.title: Styles​
searchDocs.content: The stylesheets are SCSS under packages/core/src/styles, written with the Sass module system (@use): britecharts.scss is the whole set, common.scss what every chart needs, and charts/<chart>.scss one chart. They compile through core's Vite build; pnpm lint:styles runs stylelint over them.

searchDocs.title: Tasks​
searchDocs.content: From the root:  Task	Descriptionpnpm test	Runs the Vitest suites of every package; pnpm test:ci is the same command as CI runs it, and pnpm test:watch watches. pnpm test:integration	Packs the three packages with pnpm's packer, installs them into the vanilla, TypeScript and React 19 consumers and checks tarball contents, require() paths, the typings and, in Chromium, that every way of loading a chart renders and every tooltip stays inside its chart. pnpm lint	ESLint over every package (pnpm lint:js) and stylelint over the styles (pnpm lint:styles). pnpm format runs oxfmt. pnpm check	Both linters, the type-check and the test suite, what CI runs. pnpm build / pnpm build:packages	Everything, or only the three published packages. pnpm demos	Serves the core, React and composed Storybooks together on ports 2001, 2002 and 2000. pnpm docs / pnpm docs:build	Serves or builds this site, after copying the READMEs in and generating the API pages from the charts' JSDoc. pnpm docs:links	Serves the built site and follows every link on it, external ones included; the Link check workflow runs it on every pull request and weekly. pnpm changeset	Records what a change does and which packages it bumps, for the release. pnpm version-packages	Applies the pending changesets: bumps versions and writes the changelogs. pnpm release	Builds the packages and publishes every non-private workspace, in dependency order.

searchDocs.title: Docs and Storybooks​
searchDocs.content: The API reference is generated: packages/docs/scripts/generate-docs.js runs jsdoc-to-markdown over packages/core/src and writes one page per chart into docs/API, and copy-readme.js brings the READMEs in. The three Storybooks build with pnpm build:demos and are deployed next to the site, under /storybook/, by scripts/compose-site.js, so composition is same-origin.

searchDocs.title: Releases​
searchDocs.content: Versions are managed with Changesets. @britecharts/core, @britecharts/wrappers and @britecharts/react are a fixed group, so they always share a version; the docs, demos and integration packages are never published. The Release workflow publishes from main once the pending changesets are applied, the Integration check gates every merge, and the Smoke workflow re-checks the published packages from npm and jsDelivr afterwards. MAINTAINING.md has the steps.

searchDocs.title: Test Driven Development​
searchDocs.content: D3.js charts are complex systems. As other Software Development projects, they start simple and become bloated at the end of the process. To overcome this, we have followed a component approach that allows us to create easily testable units.  We use Vitest as our test runner, with jsdom standing in for the browser.  To start running our tests you would need to follow these steps:  Fork the repository by clicking the fork button on GithubClone the repository with:git clone https://github.com/<your handle>/britecharts.gitGet into the repository folder and install the dependencies with:pnpm installRun the tests with:pnpm run test  This process watches the test and chart files, re-running the tests when those change.

searchDocs.title: JSDoc Generated Documentation​
searchDocs.content: JSDoc is an API documentation generator. It allows us to follow a methodology when commenting our code so that later we can automatically generate documentation from these comments. Check its getting started guide to know more about it.  We enforce jsDoc comments in our review process, hence each function should be commented. We require also to be mindful and when we change the code of a function. Please check if comments need to be updated too. This is essential, as our documentation gets generated from these JSDoc comments.

searchDocs.title: Labels​
searchDocs.content: On Britecharts, we aim to be methodical on using issue labels, offering our community a way to understand what are the issues about and their status within or development process. We use a bunch of GitHub labels. They are a mix of custom labels and the default Github labels for open-source projects. We base these labels on four main types: status labels, issue type labels, and the “other” category. Read on to learn more about them.  Status Labels​  They show at a glance the status and progress of each issuePrefixed with "status:", followed by the labelOnly one status label will be applied to any particular issue  Labels​  status:needs_triage – For all issues that need to be processed status:needs_reproducing – For bugs that need to be reproduced in order to get fixed status:needs_votes – Issue or bug fix that needs support from the community to be considered status:needs_design – Issue that needs design input to continue. status:in_progress – Issue that is being worked on right now. status:completed – Issue is completed and on main status:abandoned – Issue we won’t go ahead and implement, or that needs a “champion” to take it through status:blocked – Issue blocked by any reason (dependencies, previous work, lack of resources, etc.) The resulting Feature Flow is: Needs Triage >> Needs Votes >> Needs Design >> In Progress >> CompletedOutside the flow: Blocked || Abandoned The resulting Issue Flow is: Needs Triage >> Needs Reproducing >> Needs Votes >> In Progress >> CompletedOutside the flow: Blocked || Abandoned  Here is a diagram representing these states within the lifecycles:  Type Labels​  They show the type of the issuePrefixed with "Type:", followed by the label  Labels​  type:bug – An unexpected problem or unintended behaviortype:feature – A new feature requesttype:maintenance – A regular maintenance chore or task, including refactors, build system, CI, performance improvementstype:documentation – A documentation improvement tasktype:question – An issue or PR that needs more information or a user question  Other Labels​  Some of these are part of the standard GitHub labels and intended for OSS contributorsSome are related to the tools we use to maintain the libraryThey are not prefixed  Labels​  help wanted – Indicates we are looking for contributors on this issue.good first issue – Indicates the issue is a great one to tackle by newcomers to the project or OSS in general.dependencies – For snyk, to manage dependencies updates

searchDocs.title: PR Title and Commit Prefixes​
searchDocs.content: As we adopted the Commitizen standard, we started using @commitlint to help us enforce meaningful PR and commit titles that will help us to generate the Changelog in the future.  The allowed commit and PR prefixes map to the issue types, so they would be:  fix – Fixes an unexpected problem or unintended behaviorfeat – Adds a new featurechore – Any regular maintenance chore or task, including: refactors, build system, CI, performance improvementsdocs – A documentation improvement task

searchDocs.title: The Reusable Chart API
searchDocs.content: The Reusable Chart API The Reusable Chart API is a modular structure to create and reuse D3.js components. We saw the first example of this pattern in Mike Bostock’s seminal post Towards Reusable Charts (2012). We built Britecharts using this design pattern, so that all our components benefit from its characteristics. They are all simple, modular, reusable, composable, and testable. The pattern is based in a closure that allows us to keep properties private and define the elements of the components' API. Take a look at the code: /** * This function creates the graph using the selection as container * @param {D3Selection} _selection A d3 selection that represents * the container(s) where the chart(s) will be rendered */ function exports(_selection) { /* @param {object} _data The data to attach and generate the chart */ _selection.each(function (_data) { chartWidth = width - margin.left - margin.right; chartHeight = height - margin.top - margin.bottom; data = _data; buildScales(); buildAxis(); buildSVG(this); buildContainerGroups(); drawBars(); drawAxis(); }); } /** * Gets or Sets the margin of the chart * @param {object} _x Margin object to get/set * @return { margin | module} Current margin or Bar Chart module to chain calls * @public */ exports.margin = function (_x) { if (!arguments.length) { return margin; } margin = _x; return this; }; return exports; This piece of code returns a function that accepts a D3.js selection as input. Then, it extracts the data of that selection to build a chart, using the selection as the container. It also accepts some configuration (the margin, in this case) that we can set beforehand. To learn more about this pattern you can read this blog post on Eventbrite's Engineering Blog.
